source.title: What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning? A Mechanistic Study
source.authors: Samyak Jain; Ekdeep Singh Lubana; Kemal Oksuz; Tom Joy; Philip H. S. Torr; Amartya Sanyal; Puneet K. Dokania

record.tranche_reason: The study tests safety fine-tuning and jailbreak behavior, and argues that fine-tuning makes limited, input-dependent changes that attacks can evade. Its evidence refines the claim, but concerns synthetic safety behavior rather than recovery of targeted factual knowledge.
record.gate_note: The study tests synthetic safety fine-tuning and jailbreaks, not relearning on unrelated examples, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or the named WMDP/WHP/RMU recipes. Table A.1 reports post-fine-tuning accuracy on safe, unsafe, and attacked samples; the mechanistic analyses report changes in activations and weights. Values used to select hyperparameters are not recorded as outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study is about safety fine-tuning that teaches refusal, not about removing targeted knowledge. In a synthetic PCFG task, minGPT (about 3M parameters) is trained to output a null token on unsafe task–text combinations. 'Unlearning' is one of three refusal-training losses, a retain-minus-forget cross-entropy taken from Liu et al. 2024. By design the suppressed bijective mappings stay intact: most task tokens that are unsafe on B-dominant text are safe on A-dominant text (FB^s ⊂ FA^s, |FA^s| = 8). So the setup cannot tell deleting a capability apart from blocking it. Table A.1 therefore measures context-conditional refusal (null-token output) and how jailbreaks bypass it. It does not measure targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance or recovery of deleted facts. The weight-space analyses describe how the refusal transform is implemented, not whether knowledge was deleted or merely blocked. This is a related but different construct (shallow safety alignment), so it goes under fits_no_version. The study also tests no relearning, direction ablation, quantization or robust counter-method. WMDP and Lynch et al. are cited only as background on unlearning.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that safety fine-tuning (SSFT, DPO, unlearning) minimally transforms MLP weights so that unsafe inputs are projected into the null space of the original weights. This clusters safe and unsafe activations and lowers the model's sensitivity on unsafe inputs. Jailbreak and adversarial inputs yield activations close to safe ones and so evade the transform. They add that stronger protocols (DPO, unlearning) are harder to attack, and that safety pipelines need rethinking. Correction: the Llama corroboration is limited. Clustering is shown on Llama-2 and Llama-3. ΔW null-space alignment is shown only for Llama-2 7B chat against the pre-trained Llama-2 7B. All attack accuracies come from the synthetic setup.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthetic PCFG safety task and the unlearning objective adopted from Liu et al.; this is not a direct implementation or reproduction of the named WMDP, Who's Harry Potter?, or RMU recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type and strength; safety-fine-tuning protocol and learning rate; layer depth. Table A.1 reports substantially different attack outcomes across JB-CO-Task, JB-CO-Text, and JB-MisGen and across protocols/learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic minGPT refusal training, the Unlearning loss leaves unsafe-instruct accuracy at 5.0 (ηM) and 31.2 (ηS). JB-CO-Text raises it to 98.3 and 95.2. JB-MisGen (held-out task tokens, modelled on other languages) raises it to 98.5 and 92.3. DPO and SSFT behave similarly, with SSFT reaching 100. JB-CO-Task is weaker, 27.1 to 92.5 depending on method and learning rate (Table A.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-style safety fine-tuning, including an unlearning loss, is bypassed by competing-objective and out-of-distribution jailbreaks, with success depending on attack type and method strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-fine-tuning updates ΔW lie largely in the null space of the instruction-tuned weights and act mainly on unsafe inputs. Successful jailbreak and adversarial inputs barely engage ΔW and are processed like safe inputs. Similar null-space alignment is reported for Llama-2 7B chat against pre-trained Llama-2 7B (Fig. A.17), where ΔW mixes instruction and safety tuning. No row records the interventions: extrapolating along ΔW (α>1) lowers jailbreak success for SSFT while keeping safe accuracy, with no such trend for DPO or Unlearning (App. D, Fig. A.72). Moving or transferring ΔW from SSFT toward stronger methods also lowers attack success (Figs A.73–A.74).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety fine-tuning learns a minimal, input-selective transform that attacks evade, rather than removing the underlying capability.

record.problems: The reported attack accuracies are from a synthetic PCFG task with minGPT models. Chance performance is not stated for unsafe instruction accuracy, uncertainty estimates are not reported, and the study does not test factual-knowledge recovery, relearning, ablation, or quantization. The Llama experiments described here support mechanistic analyses but do not provide the Table A.1 attack-accuracy results.

untested.parts: Targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance and retained general ability under a knowledge-unlearning method; the task is refusal (null-token output), not knowledge removal
Not tested: no direction ablation that restores removed knowledge; the mechanistic analyses concern the refusal transform, in a setup where the capability is shared with safe inputs by design
Not tested on unlearned knowledge; jailbreaks (competing objectives, held-out task tokens, soft tokens) are tested only against refusal training
Not tested: no robust counter-method is evaluated against these attacks

record.verdict_notes: Changes from the previous verdict: (1) The five list-valued row_fixes are split into 49 single-row items (A1–A36, C1–C13). Every reader row carries undeclared versions V1/V3/V5, and each now gets versions ["none"] and state cannot_determine, keeping the earlier judgment, decided by what each row measures. (2) fits_no_version item 1: the JB-CO-Task range is corrected to 27.1–92.5 (SSFT ηS is 92.5, not 88.1). (3) The two `missing` items are removed. Their versions value 'none (related construct)' is not a declared identifier, and they bear on no version, so they don't meet the definition of missing. The intervention result moves into fits_no_version item 2, marked as not recorded by any row, with Fig. A.17 noted as base-vs-chat. Soft-token attacks have no success-rate numbers at all; Figs A.66–A.71 show only cluster, angle and Lipschitz analyses across 1–10 soft tokens. (4) authors_conclusion is corrected: ΔW null-space alignment is corroborated only on Llama-2, and Llama-3 only for clustering. (5) New row flags: the sample set of the Unsafe (Instruct) column is undefined. Its values cannot share samples with Unsafe (Null), for example SSFT ηS at 100.0 Null vs 72.8 Instruct, so the attack rows' baseline is ambiguous. C8/C10 role labels are inconsistent, and C7–C12 per-panel value wording is the reader's. Judgment kept: I considered linking the Unlearning-arm jailbreak rows (A5, A6, A11, A12) to E, since JB-MisGen models other languages. I kept T6 because the measure is refusal (null-token output), and the 'forgotten' capability is kept for safe contexts by construction, so the setup cannot distinguish deletion from blocking. The study fits the shallow-safety-alignment topic better, and Iris may revisit. Read status is 'part': the abstract, main text, conclusion, App. A–B setup, Table A.1, App. C.2, the C.3.8 text and App. D were read; the long figure-axis dumps were searched, not read line by line. No instructions to the reader were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not establish a chance-level reference for its unsafe-instruction accuracies or test whether targeted knowledge was removed from weights. It does measure safety behavior and whether attacks restore instruction-following behavior.
No fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
No activation-direction ablation. The study analyzes safety-fine-tuning weight changes and their effects on inputs, rather than directly demonstrating factual knowledge remaining in weights.

Tests synthetic competing-objective and mismatched-generalization jailbreaks, and soft-token adversarial attacks; does not test the full range of rephrasing, languages, or in-context information in the claim.
No newer method is tested for resisting the listed recovery attacks.

reader_labels.condition: Unlearning, ηM and ηS, under JB-CO-Text and JB-MisGen attacks
reader_labels.reason: Attacked unsafe-instruction accuracy is high despite low un-attacked accuracy for ηM; see A3, A5–A6, A9, A11–A12.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: DPO and SSFT, under JB-CO-Text and JB-MisGen attacks
reader_labels.reason: These comparator safety-fine-tuned models also show high instruction-following accuracy on attacked unsafe samples; see A17–A18, A23–A24, A29–A30, A35–A36.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: JB-CO-Task attacks, especially Unlearning and DPO
reader_labels.reason: Task-token attacks raise unsafe instruction accuracy, but the reported values are much lower than for text and mismatched-generalization attacks; see A4, A10, A16, A22.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic minGPT safety fine-tuning, including Unlearning
reader_labels.reason: The updates are reported to align with the original weights' null-space and to affect unsafe inputs more than safe inputs, consistent with a selective access mechanism; see C1–C2 and C7–C8.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic minGPT DPO and SSFT comparators
reader_labels.reason: The same qualitative weight-update and input-selectivity pattern is reported for these protocols; see C3–C6 and C9–C12.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: JB-CO-Text and JB-MisGen attacks across tested protocols and learning rates
reader_labels.reason: These attacks produce high unsafe instruction-following accuracy after safety fine-tuning; see A5–A6, A11–A12, A17–A18, A23–A24, A29–A30, A35–A36.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: JB-CO-Task attacks across tested protocols and learning rates
reader_labels.reason: Recovery varies by method and is weaker for Unlearning and DPO than for the text and mismatched-generalization attacks; see A4, A10, A16, A22, A28, A34.
